extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (faculty and students), NSF Graduate Fellowship applicants/reviewers, and computational-mathematics software reviewers
extracted.subtask_short: NSF graduate fellowship and software review
extracted.subtask_description: Describes (1) procedures and equity considerations used by panels and the NSF in awarding graduate fellowships, and (2) criteria and methods for evaluating symbolic/computational algebra systems via benchmark problems, timing, interface, and resource usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disregard race, sex, and handicap in deliberations
rubrics_metrics.description: lists are expected to disregard race, sex, and handicap in their deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are separate programs for minority fellowships and women in engineering, and additional financing for persons with handicaps who are successful (defined to include honorable mention) in the initial competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate programs for minority/women/handicapped applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a separate program for minority fellowships. There is a separate program for women in engineering. There is also additional financing for persons with handicaps who are successful (defined to include honorable mention) in the initial competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many students compete in both regular and special programs; special-program offerings interact with the main deliberation policy of disregarding race/sex/handicap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panelists evaluate men's and women's applications equally
rubrics_metrics.description: The panelists are sensitive to problems affecting women, but have not felt that women's applications should be evaluated differently from men's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite evaluating equally, panelists recommended setting aside extra fellowships specifically for women to address barriers and to incentivize more women to pursue mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observed factors disadvantaging women applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Women may not do as well in the evaluation process due to a number of factors: perhaps they have had a harder time finding mentors for research projects; women often score lower than men on tests; and references may be written with a bias towards men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists are sensitive to these problems; the recognition of these factors motivates consideration of targeted fellowships or outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to create extra fellowships for women in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The panelists would like to see extra fellowships set aside specifically for women. We need more highly qualified women graduate students, more women writing excellent Ph.D. theses, and more women with outstanding careers in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If interested, mathematicians should write to Division Director for Research Career Development and the Division Director for Mathematical Sciences to propose such programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty encouragement of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics faculties should not discourage good mathematics students from applying for an NSF Graduate Fellowship. It is beneficial for our profession and for students to go through the process of applying, even if the application does not result in an award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty should explicitly encourage students; applying yields early opportunity to think about graduate school, refine thinking about goals, and experience in writing about oneself and one's goals with respect to mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSF panel procedure: three unordered alphabetized lists
rubrics_metrics.description: The panelists present the NSF with three unordered, alphabetized lists. All the applicants in the first list and half the applicants in the second receive awards. The awardees in the second group are chosen by the National Science Foundation, based on geographical and other considerations. The third list is for those who will receive honorable mention along with those in group two who don't get awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the cited year the first two lists comprised six and eight percent of the applicants respectively; third list includes honorable mentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software-review test design: vendor-supplied benchmark problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the test procedure was to supply the vendor with a list of twenty problems to solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a mix of short problems and medium-length/long projects (the review included medium-length projects labelled 17, 20, and to a lesser extent 18 and 19) to assess both routine and larger-project capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing tests on standardized hardware
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing tests were done on the short problems on a 386/25 with 15 MB of RAM for all the products (since the common kernel was involved, we only tested Mathematica for DOS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report timings on a standardized reference machine; note that timing differences can diminish over product generations and may be less significant than before.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interface and usability
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate user interface quality: Maple's DOS interface (with ability to call previous commands into a full screen editor and customizable menus), Mathematica for Windows' notebook interface with word-processing and outlining features, Derive's interface, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the interface supports workflow (customizability, notebook/live-document features), and balance modern interface capabilities against resource constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness on benchmark symbolic problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Test for correctness on representative symbolic tasks: e.g., simplification of Sqrt(4+2 Sqrt(3)) and gravitational-potential problem (3c); the reviewer notes that Mathematica and Maple failed certain expected simplifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete mathematically meaningful tests to detect weaknesses in simplification, integration, and other symbolic routines; correctness matters as much or more than speed or interface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource usage and minimum/recommended system requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: All programs but Derive require a 386 or better. All but Derive recommend a coprocessor. Derive doesn't need (or use) more than 640K of RAM. The others recommend at least 2 MB of RAM, and Mathematica will perform poorly without 6 or 8 MB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating software, record hardware requirements and expected performance given typical user machines; low resource usage can be a significant advantage for some users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphics capability and interoperability
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematica's graphics are special: you get programmatic control of the graphics, links to standard graphics file types for import to desktop publishing programs, and more primitives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess graphics primitives, programmatic control, and import/export to standard file types (important for publication and desktop-publishing workflows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernel/core-language strength and library maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the core language and libraries: Reduce has a solid core and eclectic library functions; Mathematica's kernel is weak in the area of integration; Derive is improving but sometimes requires convoluted code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider maturity, breadth of library functions, core symbolic strengths and weaknesses (e.g., integration), and likelihood of future development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendor/community provision of solutions and support
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce and Derive will post the solutions on their electronic BBS (addresses provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability of vendor-provided solutions, documentation, and community resources is a factor in practical usability and adoptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about finite-base strong-pseudoprime primality tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Various widely-used software packages assert that a given integer is prime if it is a 'strong pseudoprime' for some given finite set of bases. For any given finite set of bases, there are infinitely many Carmichael numbers that are 'strong pseudoprimes' to all the bases in that set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on finite-base strong-pseudoprime checks for absolute primality; such methods can falsely identify composites as primes (users and implementers should prefer provable/stronger methods or multiple independent checks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical modular-exponentiation algorithm for base-2 pseudoprime testing
rubrics_metrics.description: To test whether 2^{n-1} = 1 (mod n) compute n-1 in base 2, compute r_j = 2^{2^j} mod n iteratively (r_0 = 2), and multiply the needed r_j values to obtain 2^{n-1} mod n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This binary-exponentiation algorithm requires no more than 20 log3 n operations (practical for many-digit numbers); it's vastly faster than naive division testing and is the practical core of base-a pseudoprime tests.
